arXiv:1902.05298v1 [math-ph] 14 Feb 2019

A stable quantum Darmois-Skitovich theorem

Javier Cuesta Email: j.cuesta@tum.de Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, Technische Universität München, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), München, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The Darmois-Skitovich theorem is a simple characterization of the normal distribution in terms of the independence of linear forms. We present here a non-commutative version of this theorem in the context of Gaussian bosonic states and show that this theorem is stable under small errors in its underlying conditions. An explicit estimate of the stability constants which depend on the physical parameters of the problem is given.

I Introduction and Summary of results

Among all characterizations of the normal distribution, the ones concerning the independence of linear forms stand out because of their simplicity. The landmark result of such classical characterizations is due to Darmois [1] and Skitovich [2]. Their theorem is a generalization to n−n-random variables and arbritrary coefficients of the following fact: if X,YX,Y are independent real-valued random variables with X+YX+Y and X−YX-Y independent, then XX and YY are normally distributed with the same variance (see Theorem 4). We will be interested in studying a quantum (read as non-commutative) version of the Darmois-Skitovich theorem, which we now write shortly as DS theorem. In this case, the role of the normal distribution is taken by Gaussian bosonic states: quantum states whose statistics is completely determined by the knowledge of the first and second moments and whose canonical observables obey the bosonic commutation relations.

Particularly noteworthy is the fact that the quantum DS theorem has a clear physical realization. Consider an arbitrary product state that passes through a beam-splitter as in figure 1. If the output state of the beam-splitter is also a product state, then the input states are Gaussian bosonic states with the same second moments. This is the content of the quantum DS-theorem. Mathematically, the content of the quantum DS theorem is given on theorem 7.

That there does not exist any two copies of identical non-Gaussian states fulfilling this is by no means trivial, since the action of a beam splitter does not create second-moment cross-correlations for an identical product of quantum states (Gaussian and non-Gaussian). This operational characterization of Gaussian states was already known[3], however without a direct reference to the DS theorem. We show this characterization for a general n−n-mode Gaussian bosonic state by means of the DS theorem. This has the advantage of a much clear statistical interpretation and a simpler proof. Additionally, we show that a beam splitter is the only non-trivial linear operation that can have a factorizable output for all identical input states (Lemma 6). The latter places the beam splitter as the basic element for detecting non-Gaussianity.

Of course in real life we cannot completely guarantee that two states are totally independent. Therefore it is crucial to study how stable the DS theorem is. This means, how does the conclusion of the quantum DS theorem changes, when we assume that the output state is not exactly a product, but is approximately close to a product state. Our main result is a proof of the stability of the quantum DS theorem for quantum states whose all statistical moments in position and momentum, including mixed moments, exist and are finite. Such states are described by the set of Schwartz density operators [4]. For independent input states whose output from a beam splitter is close in trace norm to a product state, we show that they are close in Hilbert-Schmidt norm to their respective Gaussian counterpart (i.e. the Gaussian state which has the same first and second moments). Moreover, the corresponding second moments of the input states have to be approximately close as well. A precise mathematical statement of this result is given in theorem 9. The robustness of the quantum DS theorem depends on the transmitivity of the beam-splitter, the number of modes and the largest fourth moment of the output state. We give an explicit dependence on these physical parameters in the proof of this theorem.

The layout of the paper is as follows. In the next subsection we give the basic definitions and results in continuous-variable quantum information that will be used. Section II contains the main result. We give a simple proof for the characterization of Gaussian bosonic states using the DS theorem and then proceed to state the stability of the DS theorem. Section II.2 introduces and summarizes the main properties of Schwartz operators. In section III.3 we give a full proof of the stability of the DS theorem. Finally, in section IV.1 we show some auxiliary lemmas and in the appendix V some explicit bounds are calculated in detail. They will be part of the constants appearing in the stability of the DS theorem 9.

I.1 Notation and preliminaries

We will be entirely concerned with continuous-variable systems with a discrete number nn of modes. We denote by

R:=(Q1,P1,…,Qn,Pn),R:=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{n},P_{n}), (1)

the vector of canonical operators for a quantum system and Rk,k=1,…​2​nR_{k},k=1,\ldots 2n its components. Here Ql,Pl,l=1,…​nQ_{l},P_{l},l=1,\ldots n act on the l−l-tensor factor of the Fock space ℋ=⨂k=1nL2​(ℝ)\mathcal{H}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{n}L^{2}(\reals) where L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\reals) denotes the space of Lebesgue square integrable functions on ℝ\reals. The canonical commutation relations (CCR) are defined by

[Rk,Rl]=i​σk​l,[R_{k},R_{l}]=i\sigma_{kl}, (2)

where σi​j\sigma_{ij} are the entries of the symplectic matrix

σ=⨁i=1nωwithω:=(01−10).\sigma=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{n}\omega\quad\text{with}\quad\omega:=\begin{pmatrix}{}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix}. (3)

We frequently use the shorthand notation Rξ:=ξ⋅σ​R,ξ∈ℝ2​nR_{\xi}:=\xi\cdot\sigma R,\qquad\xi\in\reals^{2n}. The phase-space description of a quantum state ρ\rho is determined by the characteristic function χ:ℝ2​n→ℂ\chi:\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C} defined by

χ⁡(ξ):=Tr⁡[Wξ​ρ],\chi(\xi):=\Tr[W_{\xi}\rho], (4)

where Wξ=ei​ξ⋅σ​RW_{\xi}=e^{i\xi\cdot\sigma R} is the so-called Weyl operator. The CCR are encoded in the Weyl relation

WξWη=e−i2ξ⋅σηWξ+η,ξ,η∈ℝ2​n.W_{\xi}W_{\eta}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}\xi\cdot\sigma\eta}\ W_{\xi+\eta},\quad\quad\xi,\eta\in\reals^{2n}. (5)

The name of characteristic function for the map in Eq. (4) comes from an analogy with the classical characteristic function which is the Fourier transform of a probability distribution. In fact by taking a fixed direction in phase space we recover the classical characteristic function and from there, we can “import” all the known results of the classical world. This indeed, will be used in order to give a simple proof of the characterization of Gaussian bosonic states. The condition for a function χ:ℝ2​n→ℂ\chi:\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C} to be a bona-fide quantum characteristic function is the property of sigma-positiveness. For clarity we state these results and refer the reader to Ref. 5, section 5.4 for a proof.

Theorem 1 (Quantum Bochner-Khinchin).

For χ:ℝ2​n→ℂ\chi:\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C} to be a characteristic function of a quantum state, the following conditions are necessary and sufficient:

  1. 1.

    χ⁡(0)=1\chi(0)=1 and χ\chi is continuous at ξ=0\xi=0,

  2. 2.

    χ\chi is σ\sigma-positive definite, i.e. for any m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, any set {ξ1,ξ2,…,ξm}\{\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\ldots,\xi_{m}\} of vectors in ℝ2​n\reals^{2n}, and any set {c1,c2,…,cm}\{c_{1},c_{2},\ldots,c_{m}\} of complex numbers

    ∑k,l=1mck​cl¯​χ​(ξk−ξl)​ei2​ξk⋅σ​ξl≥0\sum_{k,l=1}^{m}c_{k}\overline{c_{l}}\ \chi(\xi_{k}-\xi_{l})\ e^{\frac{i}{2}\xi_{k}\cdot\sigma\xi_{l}}\geq 0 (6)
Corollary 2 (Classical Marginals).

Let χ⁡(ξ)\chi(\xi) be the characteristic function of a quantum state. Then for every fixed ξ∈ℝ2​n\xi\in\reals^{2n} the function

ℝ∋t↦χ⁡(t​ξ),\reals\ni t\mapsto\chi(t\xi),

is a classical characteristic function, i.e. the Fourier transform of a classical probability distribution.

As in the classical case, the characteristic function is a moment generating function. The displacement vector is defined by the entries dk:=Tr⁡[ρ​Rk]d_{k}:=\Tr[\rho R_{k}] and we say that the state is centered if d=0d=0. The covariance matrix (CM) is defined by the matrix entries Γk​l=Tr⁡[ρ⁡{Rk−dk,Rl−dl}]\varGamma_{kl}=\Tr[\rho\{R_{k}-d_{k},R_{l}-d_{l}\}]. In order that Γ\varGamma corresponds to a genuine quantum CM the CCR impose the further condition [6, 7] Γ+i​σ≥0\varGamma+i\sigma\geq 0, which is nothing but the uncertainty principle expressed in a coordinate-free form.

A Gaussian bosonic state is defined as a state with a Gaussian characteristic function

χ⁡(ξ)=exp​[−ξ⋅Γ​ξ4+i​ξ⋅d].\chi(\xi)=\text{exp}[-\frac{\xi\cdot\varGamma\xi}{4}+i\xi\cdot d]. (7)

The Wigner phase space distribution is defined to be the (symplectic) Fourier transform of the characteristic function

II Main result

In the next subsections we present the quantum version of the DS theorem and our main stability result. The detailed proof of the stability of the DS theorem is presented in section III.3.

II.1 Quantum Darmois-Skitovich theorem

We are interested in a quantum analogue of the following theorem.

Theorem 4 (Darmois-Skitovich).

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} (n≥2n\geq 2) be independent random variables and a1,…,an,b1,…,bn∈ℝ\{0}a_{1},\ldots,a_{n},b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}\in\reals\backslash\{0\}. If the two linear forms

Y1=∑iai​XiandY2=∑ibi​Xiare independent,Y_{1}=\sum_{i}a_{i}X_{i}\quad\text{and}\quad Y_{2}=\sum_{i}b_{i}X_{i}\quad\text{are independent,} (12)

then XiX_{i} is normally distributed.

Different proofs and the history of the classical DS theorem can be found in p. 78 in Ref. 9 and in Ref. 10. Our setup for the quantum version is the following. We consider two n−n-mode quantum states ρ1,ρ2∈𝔅⁡(ℋ)\rho_{1},\rho_{2}\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}) with respective canonical operators

R1=(Q1,P1,…,Qn,Pn)R2=(Qn+1,Pn+1,…,Q2​n,P2​n)\begin{split}R_{1}&=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{n},P_{n})\\ R_{2}&=(Q_{n+1},P_{n+1},\ldots,Q_{2n},P_{2n})\end{split} (13)

and write R=(R1,R2)R=(R_{1},R_{2}). We assume that ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} are independent so that their state in 𝔅⁡(ℋ⊗ℋ)\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}) is a product state ρ1⊗ρ2\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}. We refer to ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} as input states.

The action of producing linear forms of random variables can be mimiced by (Gaussian) unitary evolutions USU_{S}. These unitary evolutions are generated by Hamiltonians that are quadratic expressions in the canonical operators. Moreover[8], the unitary evolution US∈𝔅⁡(ℋ⊗ℋ)U_{S}\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}) is associated with a symplectic transformation S∈S​p​(4​n,ℝ)S\in Sp(4n,\reals). In other words, the linear trasformation

R↦S​RS∈S​p​(4​n,ℝ),R\mapsto SR\qquad\qquad\qquad S\in Sp(4n,\reals), (14)

corresponds to a unitary evolution ρ↦US​ρ​US∗\rho\mapsto U_{S}\rho U^{*}_{S}.

In order to obtain an analogue of Eq. (12), we classify the set of unitaries USU_{S} which produce a bipartite independent output, i.e. such that

US​(ρ1⊗ρ2)​US∗=ρa⊗ρb,U_{S}(\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2})U^{*}_{S}=\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b}, (15)

where ρa,ρb∈𝔅⁡(ℋ)\rho_{a},\rho_{b}\in\mathfrak{B}(\mathcal{H}) are n−n-mode quantum states. This is equivalent to classifying the respective set of symplectic transformation for which Eq. (15) holds. If we are to expect that USU_{S} preserves independence, the transformation SS should at least preserve uncorrelated inputs (a generally weaker condition than independence which only deals with the second moments). Furthermore, acting locally on each state or swapping them are trivial operations which preserve independence for arbitrary states. So we need to consider other operations in order to obtain a meaningful statement for the quantum DS theorem. The following two lemmas show in fact that there is only one non-trivial symplectic transformation for our setup.

Lemma 5.

Let S∈S​p​(4​n,ℝ)S\in Sp(4n,\mathbb{R}) be such that

S​(Γ100Γ2)​ST=(⋅00∗)for all CMΓ1,Γ2∈ℝ2​n×2​n.S\begin{pmatrix}{}\varGamma_{1}&0\\ 0&\varGamma_{2}\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\ 0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{for all CM}\quad\varGamma_{1},\varGamma_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}.

Here ∗,⋅*,\cdot denote any CM∈ℝ2​n×2​n\text{CM}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}. Then SS is either of the form (A00D)\begin{pmatrix}{}A&0\\ 0&D\end{pmatrix} or (0BC0)\begin{pmatrix}{}0&B\\ C&0\end{pmatrix} with A,B,C,D∈S​p​(2​n,ℝ)A,B,C,D\in Sp(2n,\reals).

If we consider identical inputs we obtain:

Lemma 6.

Let S∈S​p​(4​n,ℝ)S\in Sp(4n,\mathbb{R}) be such that

S​(Γ00Γ)​ST=(⋅00∗)for all CMΓ∈ℝ2​n×2​n.S\begin{pmatrix}{}\varGamma&0\\ 0&\varGamma\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\ 0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{for all CM}\quad\varGamma\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}. (16)

Here ∗,⋅*,\cdot denote any CM∈ℝ2​n×2​n\text{CM}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}. Then

S=(X00Y)​11+α2​(𝟙2​nα​𝟙2​n−α​𝟙2​n𝟙2​n),=(0XY0)​11+γ2​(𝟙2​n−γ​𝟙2​nγ​𝟙2​n𝟙2​n),\begin{split}S&=\begin{pmatrix}{}X&0\\ 0&Y\end{pmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\alpha^{2}}}\begin{pmatrix}{}\iden_{2n}&\alpha\iden_{2n}\\ -\alpha\iden_{2n}&\iden_{2n}\end{pmatrix},\\ &=\begin{pmatrix}{}0&X\\ Y&0\end{pmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\gamma^{2}}}\begin{pmatrix}{}\iden_{2n}&-\gamma\iden_{2n}\\ \gamma\iden_{2n}&\iden_{2n}\end{pmatrix},\end{split} (17)

where X,Y∈S​p​(2​n,ℝ)X,Y\in Sp(2n,\mathbb{R}) and α,γ∈ℝ∪{±∞}\alpha,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}.

Thus the only non-trivial linear transformation in Eq. (14) is of the form of Eq. (17). We discard the trivial operations and set α=tan⁡θ\alpha=\tan\theta in Eq. (17)

Sθ=(cos⁡θ​𝟙2​n−sin⁡θ​𝟙2​nsin⁡θ​𝟙2​ncos⁡θ​𝟙2​n),θ≠mπ/2,m=0,1,2,…,S_{\theta}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cos\theta\iden_{2n}&-\sin\theta\iden_{2n}\\ \sin\theta\iden_{2n}&\cos\theta\iden_{2n}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\theta\neq m\pi/2,\quad m=0,1,2,\ldots, (18)

which is the symplectic transformation associated to a (n−n-mode) beam splitter operation. We refer to the latter operation as a non-trivial beam splitter transformation.

Although for every covariance matrix Γ\varGamma, Sθ​(Γ⊕Γ)​SθT=(Γ⊕Γ)S_{\theta}(\varGamma\oplus\varGamma)S_{\theta}^{T}=(\varGamma\oplus\varGamma), it turns out from the DS theorem that there does not exist a non-Gaussian state ρ\rho such that USθ​(ρ⊗ρ)​USθ∗=ρ⊗ρ.U_{S_{\theta}}(\rho\otimes\rho)U^{*}_{S_{\theta}}=\rho\otimes\rho. See figure 1.

Theorem 7 (Quantum Darmois-Skitovich).

Let USU_{S} be the unitary operation corresponding to a non-trivial beam spliter Eq. 18. Consider the state ρa​b=US​(ρ1⊗ρ2)​US∗\rho_{ab}=U_{S}(\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2})U_{S}^{*} obtained after the unitary evolution of an arbitrary product state. If the output state is a product state ρa​b=ρa⊗ρb\rho_{ab}=\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b}, then ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} are Gaussian bosonic states with the same CM but not necessarily same displacement vector.

Due to the 1–1 correspondence between quantum states and their characteristic function we have the following consequence.

Corollary 8.

Let χ1\chi_{1} and χ2\chi_{2} be the characteristic function of the quantum states ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} respectively, which have finite second moments. If for a fixed θ≠mπ/2,m=0,1,2,…\theta\neq m\pi/2,\quad m=0,1,2,\ldots the characteristic functions satisfy the functional equation

χ1​(cos⁡θ​ξ1+sin⁡θ​ξ2)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​ξ2−sin⁡θ​ξ1)=χ1​(cos⁡θ​ξ1)​χ1​(sin⁡θ​ξ2)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​ξ2)​χ2​(−sin⁡θ​ξ1),\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\xi_{1}+\sin\theta\xi_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\xi_{2}-\sin\theta\xi_{1})=\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\xi_{1})\chi_{1}(\sin\theta\xi_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\xi_{2})\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta\xi_{1}), (19)

for all ξ1,ξ2∈ℝ2​n\xi_{1},\xi_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}. then ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} are Gaussian bosonic states with the same CM but not necessarily same displacement vector.

An inmmediate proof of the quantum DS theorem can be obtained from its corresponding classical result and corollary 2. We recall that the latter corollary tells us that we always obtain a positive Wigner function (a classical probability distribution) from the quantum characteristic function whenever we move through a fixed direction in phase space.

Proof Theorem 7.

Using Eq. (8) the evolution of the input states can be expressed in terms of characteristic functions as Eq. (19). We fixed the direction ξ1=ξ2=ξ\xi_{1}=\xi_{2}=\xi and parametrize ξ1=t​ξ\xi_{1}=t\xi, ξ2=s​ξ\xi_{2}=s\xi with t,s∈ℝt,s\in\reals. Moreover, we introduce the classical characteristic functions χj(u):=χj(uξ),j=1,2\chi_{j}(u):=\chi_{j}(u\xi),j=1,2 with u∈ℝu\in\reals so that Eq. (19) reads

χ1​(cos⁡θ​t+sin⁡θ​s)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​s−sin⁡θ​t)=χ1​(cos⁡θ​t)​χ1​(sin⁡θ​s)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​s)​χ2​(−sin⁡θ​t).\chi_{1}(\cos\theta t+\sin\theta s)\chi_{2}(\cos\theta s-\sin\theta t)=\chi_{1}(\cos\theta t)\chi_{1}(\sin\theta s)\chi_{2}(\cos\theta s)\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta t).

This last equation is the functional version of the classical DS theorem (c.f. Eq. 8.7 of section XV.9 in Ref. 9). From this classical result it follows that χ1\chi_{1} and χ2\chi_{2} are one dimensional Gaussian characteristic functions with the same variance. We can compute the moments by taking derivates of the characteristic function to obtain that

χj​(t​ξ)=exp⁡[−t24​(ξ⋅Γ​ξ)+i​t​ξ⋅dj]j=1,2.\chi_{j}(t\xi)=\exp[-\frac{t^{2}}{4}(\xi\cdot\varGamma\xi)+it\xi\cdot d_{j}]\qquad j=1,2.

The result follows with t=1t=1. ∎

II.2 Stability

In the last section we presented an exact version of the DS theorem which brings naturally an operational characterization of Gaussian bosonic states. There, it is assumed an exact factorizability of the output state. In practice, it is impossible to assure such thesis since there are always errors in the measurements and therefore the validity of the result is not completely clear in real life. Moreover, any practical application can be inmmediatealy rule out if the conclusion is not robust against small changes in the defined conditions.

We are interested in finding to which extent the results of theorem 7 are affected if the main assumption is not exact but approximately satisfied. Before specifying the conditions of the stability of the quantum DS theorem, we briefly comment on the respective classical stability problem[11].

The stability of the classical DS theorem is due to Yu. R. Gabovich [15]. In his work, the word “approximately” is quantified in terms of the closeness of the cumulative distribution functions of the random variables. It is shown (Theorem 3 in Ref. 15) that for approximate independency the considered classical probability distributions are c(loglog(1/ε))−1/8c(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-1/8}-close to a normal distribution in the Levy metric. In this estimate there is no explicit value of the constant cc and therefore it is not known how it depends on the coefficients of the linear forms, neither on the number of random variables involved.

At the level of density operators it was proven[16] that weak operator topology is equivalent to trace-norm topology. Therefore Gabovich result and corollary 2 should imply at least in a qualitative manner that the quantum DS theorem is stable. However, we can obtain a better concrete estimate of the stability of the DS theorem by considering not just the marginals and the classical result, but rather using the entire phase space and the natural restrictions on the quantum characteristic functions. Namely, due to Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle there cannot be characteristic functions which are highly concentrated in some region of phase space. This naturally rules out ill-behaved distributions that can appear in the classical case. With no more preambules, we give a precise statement of our result.

We say that a quantum state ρa​b\rho_{ab} is an ε−\varepsilon-approximate product state if there is a product state ρa⊗ρb\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b} such that

‖ρa​b−ρa⊗ρb‖1≤ε,\left\lVert\rho_{ab}-\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon, (20)

Suppose that two independent states evolve according to the action of a beam splitter, but this time the output state is an ε−\varepsilon-approximate product state (see Fig. 2).

The following theorem describes the robustness of the quantum DS theorem.

Theorem 9 (Stability DS).

Let USU_{S} be the unitary operation corresponding to a non-trivial beam spliter charaterized in Eq. (18) and ρ1,ρ2\rho_{1},\rho_{2} density operators of two nn-mode systems with finite moments of all orders and whose CMs are Γ1\varGamma_{1} and Γ2\varGamma_{2}. Consider the output state ρa​b=US​(ρ1⊗ρ2)​US∗\rho_{ab}=U_{S}(\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2})U_{S}^{*} and define by ρ1′,ρ2′\rho^{\prime}_{1},\rho_{2}^{\prime} Gaussian bosonic states that have the same CMs and displacement vectors as ρ1,ρ2\rho_{1},\rho_{2}. If for sufficiently small ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) the output state ρa​b\rho_{ab} is ε\varepsilon-close to a product state in trace norm, then

‖ρj−ρj′‖2≤c1ε1/3+c2log⁡(1/ε),j=1,2,\left\lVert\rho_{j}-\rho^{\prime}_{j}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{1}\varepsilon^{1/3}+\frac{c_{2}}{\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}},\qquad j=1,2, (21)
‖Γ1−Γ2‖2≤c3​ε1/2,\left\lVert\varGamma_{1}-\varGamma_{2}\right\rVert_{2}\leq c_{3}\varepsilon^{1/2}, (22)

where the constants c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} and c3c_{3} (which are made explicit in the proof) depend on the transmitivity θ\theta of the beam-splitter, the number of modes nn and the second and fourth absolute moments of the output state ρa​b\rho_{ab}.

Note that under the conditions of theorem 9 we also have that the respective Wigner functions are close with the bound of Eq. (21). Furthermore, the stability result could be in principle be extended to a larger set of quantum states since Schwartz operators are dense in the set of trace class operators (see Lemma 2.5 in [4]).

Schwartz operators

We begin this section by reviewing some important facts about Schwartz operators which are the non-commutative analogue of Schwartz functions. The latter are infinite differentiable functions whose derivatives decay faster than any polynomial at infinity. The introduction of Schwartz operators allows us to handle differentiability and boundness problems in an elegant manner and it is for this reason that they play an important technical role in this paper. This class of operators was first introduced in Ref. 4, and the reader may find there a detailed exposition.

In our proof of the stability of the DS theorem, we deal with terms of the form Tr⁡[Rk​Rl​ρ​Rs​Rr]\Tr[R_{k}R_{l}\rho R_{s}R_{r}] which are a priori not necessarily well-defined on any dense domain of ρ\rho; it may happen that ρ\rho maps outside the domain of RlR_{l}. This is a common issue when dealing with unbounded operators. There is an inmense advantage when working with Schwartz operators since many regular properties for bounded operators become available for unbounded ones (e.g. “cycling under the trace” property holds). Indeed, Theorem 13 below plays a decisive role in the calculation of the constants appearing in our proof of the stability of DS theorem.

Definition 10 (Schwartz Operators).

An operator T∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) is called a Schwartz operator if

‖Pα​Qβ​T​Pα′​Qβ′‖1<∞for all ​α,α′,β,β′∈In,\left\lVert P^{\alpha}Q^{\beta}TP^{\alpha^{\prime}}Q^{\beta^{\prime}}\right\rVert_{1}<\infty\qquad\quad\text{for all }\alpha,\alpha^{\prime},\beta,\beta^{\prime}\in I_{n},

where In:={α=(α1,…,αn)|αi∈ℕ∪{0} for all i=1,…,n}I_{n}:=\{\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n})|\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,n\} is the set of multi-indices, and

Qα=Qα11⋯Qαnn,Pα=Pα11⋯Pαnn.Q^{\alpha}=Q^{\alpha_{1}}_{1}\cdots Q^{\alpha_{n}}_{n},\qquad\quad P^{\alpha}=P^{\alpha_{1}}_{1}\cdots P^{\alpha_{n}}_{n}. (23)

The set of all Schwartz operators will be denoted by 𝔖⁡(ℋ)\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}).

So for Schwartz-density operators all the statistical moments in QQ and PP exist and are finite. We denote by

𝒮⁡(ℋ):={ρ∈𝔖⁡(ℋ)|ρ​ is a density operator}\mathscr{S}(\mathcal{H}):=\{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H})\ |\ \rho\text{ is a density operator}\ \}

the space of density operators which are also Schwartz operators. For ρ∈𝒮⁡(ℋ)\rho\in\mathscr{S}(\mathcal{H}) we have the following neat characterization

Proposition 11.

Let TT be a Hilbert-Schmidt operator. Then T is a Schwartz operator if and only if the respective Weyl transform is a Schwartz function.

Corollary 12.

A density operator ρ\rho is a Schwartz operator if and only if its characteristic function χ\chi, or Wigner function 𝒲\mathcal{W}, is a Schwartz function. Moreover, the partial trace of a Schwartz-density operator is a Schwartz operator.

The following Theorem contains the basic properties of Schwartz operators that we use.

Theorem 13.

Let ℋ=L2​(ℝ2​n)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\reals^{2n}) and T∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}). Then

  1. (i)

    Let ff be a polynomial function on the entries of the vector R=(Q1,P1,…,Qn,Pn)R=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{n},P_{n}) and {Wξ}\{W_{\xi}\} a Weyl system. If T∈𝔖⁡(ℋ)T\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}), then Tr⁡[f⁡(R)​T]=Tr⁡[T​f​(R)]\Tr[f(R)T]=\Tr[Tf(R)]. Moreover, f⁡(R)​T∈𝔖⁡(ℋ)f(R)T\in\mathfrak{S}(\mathcal{H}) and Tr⁡[Wξ​f​(R)​T]=Tr⁡[f⁡(R)​T​Wξ]=Tr⁡[T​Wξ​f​(R)]\Tr[W_{\xi}f(R)T]=\Tr[f(R)TW_{\xi}]=\Tr[TW_{\xi}f(R)].

III.3 Proof of the stability of DS theorem 9

The proof involves a series of steps. We first use Parseval’s theorem to express the distance of the quantum states in terms of the L2−L_{2}-distance of their respective characteristic functions. Next, we show that there is a ball 𝔅r\mathfrak{B}_{r} around the origin of phase space where the characteristic functions do not vanish. The radius of this ball scales inversely proportional to the largest variance of the input states and proportional to log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon). Thus the smaller the error parameter ε\varepsilon the bigger this region is. We then proceed to bound the distance separately on 𝔅r\mathfrak{B}_{r} and its complement 𝔅rc\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r}. For the latter region, we exploit the relation between the tails of a distribution and the finiteness of it moments. Inside 𝔅r\mathfrak{B}_{r}, the problem is equivalent to the stability of the Gaussian functional Eq. (19) with restricted convex domain. For that matter, the stability of the Gaussian functional equation is reduced to the stability of the fundamental functional equation, namely the Cauchy functional equation.

We may assumed without lost of generality that the input states (and therefore the output states) are centered. This is justified by the fact that the trace and HS norms are unitarily invariant and the operation of “Gaussification” (the operation on bosonic quantum states which produces Gaussian states with the same first and second moments of the input state) commutes with the displacement operation ρ↦Wd​ρ​Wd∗\rho\mapsto W_{d}\rho W^{*}_{d}.

We denote by χa​b,χa\chi_{ab},\chi_{a} and χb\chi_{b} the characteristic functions of ρa​b,ρa\rho_{ab},\rho_{a} and ρb\rho_{b}, respectively. From Lemma (17), we have ‖g‖1≤3​ε\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\varepsilon. Let η1,η2∈ℝ2​n\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in\reals^{2n} and R1,R2R_{1},R_{2} be vectors of canonical operators as in Eq. 13. We write

G⁡(η1,η2):=Tr⁡[ei​η1⋅σ​R1⊗ei​η2⋅σ​R2​g]=χa​b​(η1,η2)−χa​(η1)​χb​(η2).G(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=\Tr[e^{i\eta_{1}\cdot\sigma R_{1}}\otimes e^{i\eta_{2}\cdot\sigma R_{2}}g]=\chi_{ab}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-\chi_{a}(\eta_{1})\chi_{b}(\eta_{2}). (36)

Now, using the covariant property of Gaussian unitary operations Eq. (8)

χρa​b​(ξ)=χρ1⊗ρ2​(SθT​ξ),\chi_{\rho_{ab}}(\xi)=\chi_{\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}}(S^{T}_{\theta}\xi),

and the fact that G⁡(η1,0)=G⁡(0,η2)=0G(\eta_{1},0)=G(0,\eta_{2})=0, we write for all η1,η2∈ℝ2​n\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in\reals^{2n} the dynamical process in terms of characteristic functions as

χ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)=χ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)​χ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)​χ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)+G⁡(η1,η2).\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})\chi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})+G(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}). and ρ2\rho_{2} and define

r:=1λ​log2​1ε1/12.r:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}\log_{2}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{1/12}}}. (38)

Then for η∈𝔅r:={ξ|‖ξ‖2≤r}\eta\in\mathfrak{B}_{r}:=\left\{\xi\ |\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq r\right\}

|χi​(η)|≥12​ε1/12i=1,2.|\chi_{i}(\eta)|\geq 12\varepsilon^{1/12}\qquad\text{i=1,2.} (39)

The choice of exponent 1/12{1/12} for ε\varepsilon in Eq. (38) will become clear in the estimates done in section V.

We divide phase space in two separating regions. One where the characteristic functions do not vanish, namely inside the ball 𝔅r:={ξ|‖ξ‖22≤r2}\mathfrak{B}_{r}:=\left\{\xi\ |\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}_{2}\leq r^{2}\right\}, and its complement which we denote by 𝔅rc\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r}. So that with the help of Parseval’s theorem, we express the distance between the two states as

(2​π)n​‖ρ1−ρ1′‖22=‖χ1−Φ‖22=∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ+∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ.\begin{split}(2\pi)^{n}\left\lVert\rho_{1}-\rho^{\prime}_{1}\right\rVert^{2}_{2}&=\left\lVert\chi_{1}-\Phi\right\rVert^{2}_{2}\\ &=\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi+\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi.\end{split} (40)

We compute the bound for 𝔅r/2\mathfrak{B}_{r/2} and 𝔅r/2c\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2} separately.

Bound on the region where the characteristic function might vanish

We use |z1−z2|2≤(|z1|2+|z2|2)/2|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\leq(|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2})/2 for z1,z2∈ℂz_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C} to express the bound as

∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ≤12​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ+12​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ.\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)|^{2}d\xi\leq\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi+\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\Phi(\xi)|^{2}d\xi. (41)

For the first term of the RHS of Eq. (41) we use that 1<2​‖ξ‖2/r1<2\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}/r for ξ∈𝔅r/2c\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2} so that

∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ≤4r2​∫ξ∈ℝ2​n‖ξ‖22​|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ.\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi\leq\frac{4}{r^{2}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}_{2}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi. (42)

Let us denote by 𝒲⁡(η)\mathcal{W}(\eta) the Wigner function of |χ1​(ξ)|2|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2} (the product of two characteristic functions is a characteristic function),

𝒲⁡(η)=1(2​π)2​n​∫ξ∈ℝ2​nei​η⋅σ​ξ​|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ.\mathcal{W}(\eta)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}e^{i\eta\cdot\sigma\xi}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi. (43)

It can be easily verified by direct computation, that the characteristic function |χ1​(ξ)|2|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2} is centered and has CM 2​Γ12\varGamma_{1}. Moreover, we have

∫ξ∈ℝ2​n‖ξ‖22|χ1(ξ)|2dξ=−(2π)n∑k=12​n∂2𝒲⁡(0)∂ηk2,\int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}_{2}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi=-(2\pi)^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta^{2}_{k}}, (44)

where ηk\eta_{k} are the components of the vector η\eta in an arbitrary but fixed basis.

We use now the representation of the Wigner function in terms of the expectation values of the parity operator[19] 𝒫\mathcal{P}

𝒲⁡(η)=1πn​Tr⁡[ρ​Wη​𝒫​W−η],\mathcal{W}(\eta)=\frac{1}{\pi^{n}}\Tr[\rho W_{\eta}\mathcal{P}W_{-\eta}], (45)

where ρ\rho is the density operator corresponding to the characteristic function |χ1​(ξ)|2|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}. The operator ρ\rho is clearly Schwartz as its characteristic function is a Schwartz function (corollary 12). The parity operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the n-fold tensor product of the parity operators for a single degree of freedom and is the unitary operator that satisfies

𝒫​Wξ​𝒫∗=W−ξ,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}W_{\xi}\mathcal{P}^{*}=W_{-\xi},
𝒫​Rk​𝒫∗=−Rk,\displaystyle\mathcal{P}R_{k}\mathcal{P}^{*}=-R_{k},
𝒫=𝒫∗=𝒫−1.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{*}=\mathcal{P}^{-1}.

Using Eq. (45) and Eq. (26) we compute

∂2𝒲⁡(0)∂ηk​∂ηl=−2πn​Tr⁡[𝒫​ρ​{Rηl,Rηk}].\frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta_{k}\partial\eta_{l}}=-\frac{2}{\pi^{n}}\Tr[\mathcal{P}\rho\{R_{\eta_{l}},R_{\eta_{k}}\}]. (46)

Thus from Eq. (42), (44) and Eq. (46) we find that

∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ≤2n+4r2​∑k=12​nTr⁡[𝒫​ρ​Rk2].\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi\leq\frac{2^{n+4}}{r^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\Tr[\mathcal{P}\rho R^{2}_{k}]. (47)

Hence, we just need to bound the terms Tr⁡[𝒫​ρ​Rk2]\Tr[\mathcal{P}\rho R^{2}_{k}]. In order to do this, we notice that 𝒫​ρ=ρ​𝒫\mathcal{P}\rho=\rho\mathcal{P}. Indeed,

𝒫​ρ=𝒫​1(2​π)n​∫|χ⁡(ξ)|2​W−ξ​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\rho=\mathcal{P}\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int|\chi(\xi)|^{2}W_{-\xi}d\xi =1(2​π)n​∫|χ⁡(ξ)|2​Wξ​𝑑ξ​𝒫,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int|\chi(\xi)|^{2}W_{\xi}d\xi\;\mathcal{P},
=1(2​π)n​∫|χ⁡(ξ)|2​W−ξ​𝑑ξ​𝒫=ρ​𝒫.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int|\chi(\xi)|^{2}W_{-\xi}d\xi\;\mathcal{P}=\rho\mathcal{P}.

Moreover, from the spectral decomposition of ρ\rho we have 𝒫​ρ=ρ​𝒫\mathcal{P}\sqrt{\rho}=\sqrt{\rho}\>\mathcal{P}. Accordingly,

Tr⁡[𝒫​ρ​Rk2]\displaystyle\Tr[\mathcal{P}\rho R^{2}_{k}] =Tr⁡[𝒫​ρ​Rk2​ρ],\displaystyle=\Tr[\mathcal{P}\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{k}\sqrt{\rho}],
≤‖ρ​Rk2​ρ‖1,\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{k}\sqrt{\rho}\right\rVert_{1},
=Tr⁡[ρ​Rk2].\displaystyle=\Tr[\rho R_{k}^{2}].

Here we have used the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the cyclicity of the trace that comes from the properties of the Schwartz operator ρ\rho; see Theorem 13 (i),(i​i),(i​v)(i),(ii),(iv).

In summary, we have the following bound for the tails of our characteristic function

∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}d\xi ≤2n+4r2​Tr⁡Γ1,\displaystyle\leq\frac{2^{n+4}}{r^{2}}\Tr\varGamma_{1},
=(2n+4​12​λ​Tr⁡Γ1)​1log⁡1ε.\displaystyle=\left(2^{n+4}12\lambda\Tr\varGamma_{1}\right)\frac{1}{\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}.

Since Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) has the same CM as χ⁡(ξ)\chi(\xi) we can use the same bound to obtain

1(2​π)n​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2c|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)|^{2}d\xi ≤(192​λ​Tr⁡Γ1πn)​1log⁡1ε,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{192\lambda\Tr\varGamma_{1}}{\pi^{n}}\right)\frac{1}{\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}},
≤c22log⁡1ε,\displaystyle\leq\frac{c^{2}_{2}}{\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}, (48)

where

c2:=8​3​λ​Tr⁡Γa​bπn,c_{2}:=8\sqrt{\frac{3\lambda\Tr\varGamma_{ab}}{\pi^{n}}}, (49)

and Γa​b\varGamma_{ab} is the CM of the output state ρa​b\rho_{ab}. Note that since the BS is a passive transformation, the trace of the input CM, Γ1⊕Γ2\varGamma_{1}\oplus\varGamma_{2}, is the same as the trace of the output CM Γa​b\varGamma_{ab}. Thus is clear that Tr⁡Γ1≤Tr⁡Γa​b\Tr\varGamma_{1}\leq\Tr\varGamma_{ab}.

Bound inside the region where χ\chi does not vanish:

We proceed to compute the bound for the first term of the RHS of Eq. (40) following the ideas of Ref. 13, 14, 15. For that matter, let η1,η2∈ℝ2​n\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in\reals^{2n} with ‖ηj‖2<r/2\left\lVert\eta_{j}\right\rVert_{2}<r/2 so that cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2,cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1∈𝔅r\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2},\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1}\in\mathfrak{B}_{r}. Let us take the logarithm (principal branch) on both sides of Eq. (37). We write

Ψ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)+Ψ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)=Ψ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)+Ψ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)+Ψ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)+Ψ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)+Q⁡(η1,η2),\Psi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\Psi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})+\Psi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})+Q(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}), (50)

where Ψj​(η):=−log⁡χj​(η)\Psi_{j}(\eta):=-\log\chi_{j}(\eta) for j=1,2j=1,2 and

Q⁡(η1,η2):=−log⁡(1+G⁡(η1,η2)χ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)​χ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)​χ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)​χ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)).Q(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=-\log\left(1+\frac{G(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})}{\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})\chi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})}\right). (51)

Since ρj,j=1,2\rho_{j},j=1,2 is Schwartz, we can define continuous vector-valued functions ϕj​(ξ):𝔅r/2→ℂ2​n\phi_{j}(\xi):\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n} by

ϕj​(ξ):=∇Ψj​(ξ).\phi_{j}(\xi):=\nabla\Psi_{j}(\xi).

Note that ϕj​(ξ),j=1,2,\phi_{j}(\xi),j=1,2, are in fact conservative vector fields and that ϕj​(0)=0\phi_{j}(0)=0 as ρj\rho_{j} is centered. The gradient of ϕj\phi_{j} is the Hessian of χj\chi_{j} (see Lemma 14) and 2∇ϕj(0)=σΓjσT2\nabla\phi_{j}(0)=\sigma\varGamma_{j}\sigma^{T} for j=1,2j=1,2.

Inhomogeneous Cauchy Functional Equation

Next, we want to obtain a functional equation only depending on χ1\chi_{1} or χ2\chi_{2}. In order to do so, we differentiate Eq. (50) in the direction of η1\eta_{1} to find

cos⁡θ​ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)−sin⁡θ​ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)=cos⁡θ​ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)−sin⁡θ​ϕ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)+Q1​(η1,η2),\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})+Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}), (52)

where Q1​(η1,η2):=d​Q​(η1+t​η1,η2)d​t|t=0Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=\frac{dQ(\eta_{1}+t\eta_{1},\eta_{2})}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}. We evaluate in Eq. (52) η1=0\eta_{1}=0 to get

cos⁡θ​ϕ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)−sin⁡θ​ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)=Q1​(0,η2),\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})=Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2}), (53)

In a similar fashion we differentiate Eq. (50) in the direction of η2\eta_{2} and set to zero to obtain

sin⁡θ​ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)+cos⁡θ​ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)=sin⁡θ​ϕ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)+cos⁡θ​ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)+Q2​(η1,η2),\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})+Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}), (54)
sin⁡θ​ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)+cos⁡θ​ϕ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)=Q2​(η1,0),\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0), (55)

where Q2​(η1,η2):=d​Q​(η1,η2+t​η2)d​t|t=0Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=\frac{dQ(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}+t\eta_{2})}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}.

Now we will be able to decouple ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2}. First, we substract Eq. (53) from Eq. (52) and Eq. (55) from Eq. (54) to obtain

[ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)−ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)−ϕ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)]=tan⁡θ⁡[ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)−ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)−ϕ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)]+Q1​(η1,η2)−Q1​(0,η2)cos⁡θ,\begin{split}[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]&=\tan\theta[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]\\ &+\frac{Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})}{\cos\theta},\end{split} (56)
[ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)−ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)−ϕ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)]=−tan⁡θ⁡[ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)−ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)−ϕ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)]+Q2​(η1,η2)−Q2​(η1,0)cos⁡θ.\begin{split}[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]&=-\tan\theta[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]\\ &+\frac{Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)}{\cos\theta}.\end{split} (57)

Thus from Eq. (56) and (57) we find the following inhomogeneous Cauchy equations

[ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1+sin⁡θ​η2)−ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)−ϕ1​(sin⁡θ​η2)]=sin⁡θ⁡[Q2​(η1,η2)−Q2​(η1,0)]+cos⁡θ⁡[Q1​(η1,η2)−Q1​(0,η2)],\begin{split}[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]&=\sin\theta[Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)]\\ &+\cos\theta[Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})],\end{split} (58)
[ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2−sin⁡θ​η1)−ϕ2​(cos⁡θ​η2)−ϕ2​(−sin⁡θ​η1)]=sin⁡θ⁡[Q1​(η1,η2)−Q1​(0,η2)]+cos⁡θ⁡[Q2​(η1,η2)−Q2​(η1,0)].\begin{split}[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]&=\sin\theta[Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})]\\ &+\cos\theta[Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)].\end{split} (59)

Bound on 𝔅r/2\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}

Now that ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2} are decoupled, we continue only with ϕ1\phi_{1} as with ϕ2\phi_{2} is analogous and the same upper bound is obtained. We recall that the derivative of a vector with respect to a vector can be represented as a matrix. Thus when we differentiate Eq. (58) in the direction of η2\eta_{2} and evaluate at η2=0\eta_{2}=0, we obtain the following matrix-valued equation

∇ϕ1​(cos⁡θ​η1)−σ​Γ1​σT2+Q12​(0,0)tan⁡θ=Q22​(η1)+Q12​(η1)tan⁡θ.\nabla\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\frac{\sigma\varGamma_{1}\sigma^{T}}{2}+\frac{Q_{12}(0,0)}{\tan\theta}=Q_{22}(\eta_{1})+\frac{Q_{12}(\eta_{1})}{\tan\theta}. (60)

Here Q12​(η1,0):ℝ2​n→ℂ2​n×2​nQ_{12}(\eta_{1},0):\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n} and Q22​(η1,0):ℝ2​n→ℂ2​n×2​nQ_{22}(\eta_{1},0):\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n} are defined as

Q12​(η1,0):=∂2Q⁡(η1+t​η1,s​η2)∂s​∂t|s=t=0andQ22​(η1):=∂2Q⁡(η1,s​η2+t​η2)∂s​∂t|s=t=0.Q_{12}(\eta_{1},0):=\frac{\partial^{2}Q(\eta_{1}+t\eta_{1},s\eta_{2})}{\partial s\partial t}\Bigr|_{s=t=0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_{22}(\eta_{1}):=\frac{\partial^{2}Q(\eta_{1},s\eta_{2}+t\eta_{2})}{\partial s\partial t}\Bigr|_{s=t=0}. (61)

Accordingly, we integrate the previous equation twice from zero to η\eta, ‖η‖2≤r/2\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{2}\leq r/2. We obtain for ξ∈𝔅r/2\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}

χ1(ξ)=exp[−ξ⋅(σ​Γ1​σT4−V2)ξ−F(ξcos⁡θ)],\chi_{1}(\xi)=\exp[-\xi\cdot\left(\frac{\sigma\varGamma_{1}\sigma^{T}}{4}-\frac{V}{2}\right)\xi-F\left(\frac{\xi}{\cos\theta}\right)], (62)

with

V:=−Q12​(0,0)tan⁡θ=σ⁡(Tr⁡g​R1​R2T)​σTtan⁡θ,V:=-\frac{Q_{12}(0,0)}{\tan\theta}=\frac{\sigma(\Tr gR_{1}R_{2}^{T})\sigma^{T}}{\tan\theta},
F⁡(ξ):=cos2⁡θ​∫𝒞⁡(ξ)(∫𝒞⁡(η)(Q22​(η1)+Q12​(η1)tan⁡θ)⋅d​η1)⋅𝑑η,F(\xi):=\cos^{2}\theta\int_{\mathcal{C}(\xi)}\left(\int_{\mathcal{C}(\eta)}\left(Q_{22}(\eta_{1})+\frac{Q_{12}(\eta_{1})}{\tan\theta}\right)\cdot d\eta_{1}\right)\cdot d\eta,

where 𝒞⁡(ξ),𝒞⁡(η)\mathcal{C}(\xi),\mathcal{C}(\eta) are curves in phase space connecting the origin with the vectors ξ\xi and η\eta. Moreover, these last terms can be upper bounded by (see Appendix on section V)

‖V‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2} ≤(24​n2​κ|tan⁡θ|)​ε,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt{24n^{2}\kappa}}{|\tan\theta|}\right)\sqrt{\varepsilon}, (63)
|F⁡(ξcos⁡θ)|2\displaystyle\left|F\left(\frac{\xi}{\cos\theta}\right)\right|^{2} ≤(n2​κ​‖ξ‖242​tan2⁡θ)​ε2/3,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{n^{2}\kappa\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}}{2\tan^{2}\theta}\right)\varepsilon^{2/3}, (64)

where the largest absolute fourth moment of ρa​b\rho_{ab} is defined as

κ:=max⁡{‖ρa​b​Rξ2​Rη2‖1|‖ξ‖2=‖η‖2=1}.\kappa:=\max\left\{\left\lVert\rho_{ab}R^{2}_{\xi}R^{2}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{1}\;\big|\;\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{2}=1\right\}. (65)

At this point we can show that the CM of ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} are ε−\varepsilon-close. From differentiating Eq. (53) with respect to η2\eta_{2} and evaluating at zero, we get the relation between the CMs of ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2},

Γ1−Γ2=2cos2⁡θ​V.\varGamma_{1}-\varGamma_{2}=\frac{2}{\cos^{2}\theta}V.

Hence, from Eq. (63)

‖Γ1−Γ2‖2≤(384​n2​κ|sin⁡2​θ|)​ε.\left\lVert\varGamma_{1}-\varGamma_{2}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt{384n^{2}\kappa}}{|\sin 2\theta|}\right)\ \sqrt{\varepsilon}. (66)

Now we can proceed to show that for ξ∈𝔅r/2\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}, the characteristic function of the state ρ1\rho_{1} is ε−\varepsilon-close to the Gaussian characteristic function Φ=exp[−ξ⋅Γ1ξ/4]\Phi=\exp[-\xi\cdot\varGamma_{1}\xi/4].

We use Eq. (62), |ex−1|≤|x|​max⁡{1,eRe⁡[x]}|e^{x}-1|\leq|x|\max\left\{1,e^{\operatorname{Re}[x]}\right\} and |χ1​(ξ)|2=|Φ⁡(ξ)|2​eξ⋅V​ξ−2​Re⁡[F⁡(ξ/cos⁡θ)]|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}=|\Phi(\xi)|^{2}e^{\xi\cdot V\xi-2\operatorname{Re}[F(\xi/\cos\theta)]} to write the bound as

∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi =∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|Φ(ξ)|2|exp[ξ⋅Vξ/2−F(ξ/cosθ)]−1|2dξ\displaystyle=\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\Phi(\xi)|^{2}|\exp[\xi\cdot V\xi/2-F(\xi/\cos\theta)]-1\right|^{2}d\xi
≤∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)|2​|ξ⋅V​ξ2−F⁡(ξ/cos⁡θ)|2​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\leq\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left|\frac{\xi\cdot V\xi}{2}-F(\xi/\cos\theta)\right|^{2}d\xi,
≤12​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)|2​(|ξ⋅V​ξ|24+|F⁡(ξ/cos⁡θ)|2)​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left(\frac{|\xi\cdot V\xi|^{2}}{4}+|F(\xi/\cos\theta)|^{2}\right)d\xi
≤(4​n2​κ​ε2/3tan2⁡θ)​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)|2​‖ξ‖24​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{4n^{2}\kappa\varepsilon^{2/3}}{\tan^{2}\theta}\right)\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi, (67)

Here in the second inequality we have used again |z1−z2|2≤(|z1|2+|z2|2)/2|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\leq(|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2})/2 for z1,z2∈ℂz_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C} and in the last inequality Eq. (63) and Eq. (64). We show now that

1(2​π)n​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)|2​‖ξ‖24​𝑑ξ≤512​n2​κπn​(1+3​sin⁡2​θcos4⁡θ).\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi\leq\frac{512n^{2}\kappa}{\pi^{n}}\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\cos^{4}\theta}\right). (68)

We used again the Wigner representation, Eq.(43), of the characteristic function |χ1​(ξ)|2|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2} in order to compute the bound of Eq. (68)

1(2​π)n​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)|2​‖ξ‖24​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi ≤1(2​π)n​∫ξ∈ℝ2​n|χ1​(ξ)|2​‖ξ‖24​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi,
=1(2​π)n​∑k,l=12​n∫ξ∈ℝ2​n|χ1​(ξ)|2​ξk2​ξl2​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\ \int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\xi^{2}_{k}\xi^{2}_{l}d\xi,
=∂4𝒲⁡(0)∂ηk2​∂ηl2.\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{4}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta^{2}_{k}\partial\eta^{2}_{l}}.

Using Lemma 14 with the help of the CCR gives

∑k,l=12​n∂4𝒲⁡(0)∂ηk2​∂ηl2=8πn​∑k,l=12​nTr⁡[ρ​𝒫​{Rk2,Rl2}].\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\frac{\partial^{4}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta^{2}_{k}\partial\eta^{2}_{l}}=\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}].

Here ρ\rho is again the density operator corresponding to the characteristic function |χ⁡(ξ)|2|\chi(\xi)|^{2}. We use again that 𝒫​ρ=ρ​𝒫\mathcal{P}\rho=\rho\mathcal{P} (see subsection III.3) and Hölder’s inequality to bound

8πn​∑k,l=12​nTr⁡[ρ​𝒫​{Rk2,Rl2}]≤8πn​∑k,l=12​n(‖ρ​Rk2​Rl2​ρ‖1+‖ρ​Rl2​Rk2​ρ‖1).\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}]\leq\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\left(\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{k}R^{2}_{l}\sqrt{\rho}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{l}R^{2}_{k}\sqrt{\rho}\right\rVert_{1}\right).

Now using Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and the ciclycity properties for Schwartz operators we find

8πn​∑k,l=12​nTr⁡[ρ​𝒫​{Rk2,Rl2}]\displaystyle\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}] ≤16πn​(∑k=12​n(Tr⁡ρ​Rk4)1/2)2,\displaystyle\leq\frac{16}{\pi^{n}}\left(\sum^{2n}_{k=1}(\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k})^{1/2}\right)^{2},
≤32​nπn​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ​Rk4.\displaystyle\leq\frac{32n}{\pi^{n}}\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}. (69)

Since we want to specify all the constants in terms of the moments of the output state ρa​b\rho_{ab} we need to do the following computations. Using the explicit form of the BS transformation Eq. (18) and the derivatives of χ1​(ξ)\chi_{1}(\xi), we obtain after a tedious, but straightforward calculation

cos4⁡θ​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ1​R1​k4+sin4⁡θ​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ2​R2​k4−6​sin2⁡θ​cos2⁡θ​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ1​R1​k2​Tr​ρ2​R2​k2=∑k=12​nTr⁡ρa​b​Rk4,\cos^{4}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{1k}+\sin^{4}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{4}_{2k}-6\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{1k}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{2}_{2k}=\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{k},

which together with the positivity of the fourth moments implies

∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ1​Rk4≤6​tan2⁡θ​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ1​R1​k2​Tr​ρ2​R2​k2+1cos4⁡θ​∑k=12​nTr⁡ρa​b​Rk4.\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}\leq 6\tan^{2}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{1k}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{2}_{2k}+\frac{1}{\cos^{4}\theta}\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{k}. (70)

Moreover, the relation between the fourth moments of the symmetrized state ρ\rho and ρ1\rho_{1} is given by

TrρRk4=2Trρ1Rk4+6(Trρ1Rk2)2,k=1,…,2n.\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}=2\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}+6(\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{k})^{2},\qquad k=1,\ldots,2n. (71)

Combining Eqs. (70) and (71) and using (Tr⁡ρ1​Rk2)2≤Tr⁡ρ1​Rk4≤κ(\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{k})^{2}\leq\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}\leq\kappa we obtain

∑k=12​nTr⁡ρ​Rk4≤16​n​κ​(1+3​sin⁡2​θcos4⁡θ),\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}\leq 16n\kappa\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\cos^{4}\theta}\right),

and Eq. (69) gives the claimed bound in Eq. (68). Hence, inserting Eq. (68) in Eq. (67) we obtain the bound for the non-vanishing region 𝔅r/2\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}

1(2​π)n​∫ξ∈𝔅r/2|χ1​(ξ)−Φ⁡(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ≤c12​ε2/3,\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi\leq c^{2}_{1}\varepsilon^{2/3}, (72)

where

c1:=32​2πn​(1+3​sin⁡2​θsin⁡2​θ)​n2​κ.c_{1}:=32\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi^{n}}\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta}\right)}n^{2}\kappa. (73)

The result of the theorem follows from Eq. (48), (72) and the concavity of the square root.

IV Discussion

The DS theorem can be understood as the statement that Gaussian bosonic states with same covariance matrix are the only fixed point states of a non-trivial beam splitter transformation. In constrast with other characterizations of Gaussian states such as the one from Hudson[12], the DS theorem does not require any constraint on the purity of the state. The stability result of Theorem 9 provides an explicit estimate of the robustness of a characterization of Gaussian states through linear independence. In particular, we have obtained an estimate of the constants which reflect the fact that the quantum DS theorem is unstable when the beam-splitter is close to being transparent (θ=0\theta=0) or a mirror (θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2). The exact dependence on the transmitivity constant is shown in Fig. 3. Throughout this work, we have made an effort to present explicit constants as well as to improve the order of the error parameter; however this does not mean that they are anywhere close to optimal. In fact, it is not known to us if the optimal constant must necessarily depend on the number of modes nn or whether the log(1/ε)−1/2\log(1/\varepsilon)^{-1/2} dependence can be lifted to a polynomial dependence.

The Darmois-Skitovich theorem is not only interesting as a neat characterization problem, but also because of its practical applications: it is the main theoretical concept behind the signal reconstruction method known as blind source separation[18] which is actively studied in the field of communication and signal processing. We hope with this study of the stability of the quantum DS theorem to stimulate a further investigation of this theorem and its extensions in the quantum information community.

Lemma 16.

Let S∈G​L​(4​n,ℝ)S\in GL(4n,\mathbb{R}) such that

S​(Γ00Γ)​ST=(⋅00∗)is 2​n×2​n block diagonal for all symmetric Γ∈ℝ2​n×2​n.S\begin{pmatrix}{}\varGamma&0\\ 0&\varGamma\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\ 0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{is $2n\times 2n$ block diagonal for all symmetric $\varGamma\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$.} (74)

Then it follows that:

    SS is either of the form

    with A,B,CA,B,C and D∈ℝ2​n×2​nD\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n} invertible.

  2. (ii)
    S​(X00X)​ST=(⋅00∗)is 2​n×2​n block diagonal for all X∈ℝ2​n×2​n.S\begin{pmatrix}{}X&0\\ 0&X\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\ 0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{is $2n\times 2n$ block diagonal for all $X\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$.} (75)
Proof of Lemma 16.

We decompose S=(ABCD)S=\begin{pmatrix}{}A&B\\ C&D\end{pmatrix} into blocks A,B,CA,B,C and D∈ℝn×nD\in\reals^{n\times n} and observe that equation (74) is equivalent to

A​Γ​CT+B​Γ​DT=0for all Γ=ΓT.A\varGamma C^{T}+B\varGamma D^{T}=0\quad\text{for all $\varGamma=\varGamma^{T}$.} (76)

Using tensor notation this equation can be written[20] as

(A⊗C+B⊗D)​|Γ⟩=0for all |Γ⟩∈ℝ4​n⊗ℝ4​n symmetric.\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)|\varGamma\rangle=0\quad\quad\text{for all $|\varGamma\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}$ symmetric}.
⇔\displaystyle\iff (A⊗C+B⊗D)​P+​|X⟩=0for all |X⟩∈ℝ4​n⊗ℝ4​n.\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)P_{+}|X\rangle=0\quad\quad\text{for all $|X\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}$.}
⇔\displaystyle\iff (A⊗C+B⊗D)​P+=0.\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)P_{+}=0.
⇔P+​(AT⊗CT+BT⊗DT)=0,\iff P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes C^{T}+B^{T}\otimes D^{T})=0, (77)

where P+P_{+} denotes the projector onto the symmetric subspace of ℝ4​n⊗ℝ4​n\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}. We make the following remark that will be used frequently during this proof: the symmetrization or symmetric component of a non-zero product state does not vanish. Suppose it does, then P+​(|v⟩⊗|w⟩)=0P_{+}(|v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle)=0 and |v⟩⊗|w⟩+|w⟩⊗|v⟩=0|v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle+|w\rangle\otimes|v\rangle=0. Performing the scalar product with ⟨v|⊗⟨w|\langle v|\otimes\langle w| leads to ‖v‖2​‖w‖2+|⟨v|w⟩|2=0\left\lVert v\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert w\right\rVert^{2}+|\langle v|w\rangle|^{2}=0 which is only zero if and only if |v⟩=|w⟩=0|v\rangle=|w\rangle=0.

On (i): We now prove the first part of the Lemma by considering the two cases:
(a) One of the submatrices AA,BB,CC or DD is zero: we only treat the case A=0A=0, the others are similar. Then AT⊗CT=0A^{T}\otimes C^{T}=0 and BTB^{T} is invertible (otherwise SS would not have full rank). Since any non-zero product BT​v⊗DT​wB^{T}v\otimes D^{T}w (for some v,w∈ℝ2​nv,w\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}) would contain a non-vanishing symmetric component, equation (77) implies that DT=0D^{T}=0.

(b) We prove by contradiction that in this case the four submatrices are invertible. For instance, assume that AA is not invertible. Then there exists a vector 0≠|a⟩∈Ker​AT0\neq|a\rangle\in\text{Ker}A^{T}. We choose |e⟩∉Ker​DT|e\rangle\notin\text{Ker}D^{T} (recall that D≠0D\neq 0) and with (77) we then find

0=P+​(AT⊗CT+BT⊗DT)​|a⟩⊗|e⟩=P+​(BT​|a⟩⊗DT​|e⟩).0=P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes C^{T}+B^{T}\otimes D^{T})|a\rangle\otimes|e\rangle=P_{+}(B^{T}|a\rangle\otimes D^{T}|e\rangle). (78)

By the same argument as in (a)(a) we now conclude |a⟩∈Ker​BT|a\rangle\in\text{Ker}B^{T}. Moreover,

ST​(a0)=(ATCTBTDT)​(a0)=0.S^{T}\begin{pmatrix}a\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{T}&C^{T}\\ B^{T}&D^{T}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=0.

The latter is in contradiction to the invertibility of SS (if SS is an invertible matrix then the kernel is trivial), hence A –and due to analogous reasoning– B,CB,C and DD are invertible.

On (ii): We now proof the second part of the Lemma, Eq. (75), by showing that the equivalent expression A​X​CT+B​X​DT=0AXC^{T}+BXD^{T}=0 for all X∈ℝ2​n×2​nX\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n} is true.
This is trivially satisfied if SS is given in form of case (i,a). Therefore we are left with the case (i,b) where in particular BB and CC are invertible. W.l.o.g. we choose B=C=𝟙B=C=\iden (this can be done by redefining A→A−1​BA\to A^{-1}B and D→D−1​CD\to D^{-1}C in (76)) and equation (77) reads

P+(AT⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗DT)=0.P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T})=0. (79)

We now show in three steps that AT⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗DT=0A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T}=0, which then concludes the proof. First we show that there exists λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} such that S​p​e​c​(AT)={λ}Spec(A^{T})=\{\lambda\} and S​p​e​c​(DT)={−λ}Spec(D^{T})=\{-\lambda\}. To this purpose we choose eigenvectors |e⟩|e\rangle of ATA^{T} and |f⟩|f\rangle of and DTD^{T} with eigenvalues λ\lambda and ω\omega respectively. Then

0=P+(AT⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗DT)|e⟩⊗|f⟩=(λ+ω)P+(|e⟩⊗|f⟩).0=P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T})|e\rangle\otimes|f\rangle=(\lambda+\omega)P_{+}(|e\rangle\otimes|f\rangle).

Finally, equation (79) reads

and we can conclude the proof by deriving that this implies (NA⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗ND)=0(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})=0. This is the third step.

(NA⊗𝟙+𝟙⊗ND)=0.(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})=0. (81)

Lemma 17.

Let ρ12\rho_{12} be a density operator of a bipartite system with reduced states ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2}. If ρ1~⊗ρ2~\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}} describe an arbitrary product state and ‖ρ12−ρ1~⊗ρ2~‖1≤ε\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon, then ‖ρ12−ρ1⊗ρ2‖1≤3​ε\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\varepsilon.

≤ε+‖ρ1~⊗ρ2~−ρ1~⊗ρ2‖1+‖ρ1~⊗ρ2−ρ1⊗ρ2‖1,\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\rho_{2}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1},
=ε+‖ρ2~−ρ2‖1+‖ρ1~−ρ1‖1.\displaystyle=\varepsilon+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}-\rho_{1}\right\rVert_{1}.

Exploiting that ‖X‖1=supY:‖Y‖≤1Tr[YX]\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{1}=\sup_{Y:\left\lVert Y\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[YX] we can bound

‖ρ1~−ρ1‖1\displaystyle\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}-\rho_{1}\right\rVert_{1} =supY:‖Y‖≤1Tr[(Y⊗𝟙)(ρ1~⊗ρ2~−ρ12)],\displaystyle=\sup_{Y:\left\lVert Y\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[(Y\otimes\iden)(\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12})],
≤supY^:‖Y^‖≤1Tr[Y^(ρ1~⊗ρ2~−ρ12)],\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\hat{Y}:\left\lVert\hat{Y}\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[\hat{Y}(\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12})],
=‖ρ1~⊗ρ2~−ρ12‖1≤ϵ,\displaystyle=\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\epsilon,

and similar for the other term. ∎

Proof of Lemma (15).

for all ξ∈ℝ2​n\xi\in\reals^{2n}. Replace ξ↦(ξ/cos⁡θ)\xi\mapsto(\xi/\cos\theta) in the previous equation to obtain

|χ1​((1+tan2⁡θ)​ξ)|≥|χ1​(ξ)​‖χ1​(tan2⁡θ​ξ)‖​χ2​(tan⁡θ​ξ)|2−3​ε.\left|\chi_{1}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\right|\geq|\chi_{1}(\xi)||\chi_{1}(\tan^{2}\theta\xi)||\chi_{2}(\tan\theta\xi)|^{2}-3\varepsilon.

Similarly, for 0<θ≤π/40<\theta\leq\pi/4 and η1=−tan⁡θ​η2,η2=ξ\eta_{1}=-\tan\theta\eta_{2},\eta_{2}=\xi we arrive to

|χ2​((1+tan2⁡θ)​ξ)|≥|χ2​(ξ)​‖χ2​(tan2⁡θ​ξ)‖​χ1​(tan⁡θ​ξ)|2−3​ε.\left|\chi_{2}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\right|\geq|\chi_{2}(\xi)||\chi_{2}(\tan^{2}\theta\xi)||\chi_{1}(\tan\theta\xi)|^{2}-3\varepsilon.

With γ⁡(ξ):=minj⁡min‖η‖<‖ξ‖​|χj​(η)|\gamma(\xi):=\min_{j}\min_{\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert<\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert}\left|\chi_{j}(\eta)\right| we obtain γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)​ξ)≥γ4​(ξ)−3​ε\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\geq\gamma^{4}\left(\xi\right)-3\varepsilon. Replacing ξ\xi by (1+tan2⁡θ)k​ξ\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k}\xi with k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} in the previous equation gives

γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)k+1​ξ)≥γ4​((1+tan2⁡θ)k​ξ)−3​εfor all ​ξ∈ℝ2​n,k∈ℕ.\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\gamma^{4}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k}\xi\right)-3\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }\xi\in\reals^{2n},k\in\mathbb{N}. (82)

It is a fact that for any classical characteristic function ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) with variance λ\lambda the following inequality holds (see for instance Ref. 17, p. 89)

|ϕ⁡(t)|≥1−12​λ​t2.|\phi(t)|\geq 1-\frac{1}{2}\lambda t^{2}. (83)

Let us fix ξ\xi in the direction of phase space in which we obtain the largest variance λ\lambda of ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} and consider the region where ‖ξ‖2≤1λ\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}. Then from Eq. 83 for ‖ξ‖2≤1λ\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}} we have |χ⁡(ξ)|≥1/2|\chi(\xi)|\geq 1/2.

Using Eq. (82) and the inequality (1−a)n≥1−n​a,∀n∈ℕ,∀a∈[0,1](1-a)^{n}\geq 1-na,\forall n\in\mathbb{N},\forall a\in[0,1], we can show by induction that

γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)k+1​ξ)≥(12)4k−4​εfor ​k∈ℕ,‖ξ‖2≤1λ.\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k}}-4\varepsilon\qquad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{N},\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}.

Moreover, for ε<1\varepsilon<1 we clearly have

γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)k+1​ξ)≥(12)4k−4​ε1/12for ​k∈ℕ,‖ξ‖2≤1λ.\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k}}-4\varepsilon^{1/12}\qquad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{N},\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}. (84)

Finally, we take k0k_{0} such that 2k0=log2⁡1ε1/122^{k_{0}}=\sqrt{\log_{2}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{1/12}}}, to obtain with the help of Eq. (84)

γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)k0​ξ)\displaystyle\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\right) ≥(12)4k0−1−4​ε1/12,\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k_{0}-1}}-4\varepsilon^{1/12},
=12​ε1/12.\displaystyle=12\varepsilon^{1/12}.

We thus have γ⁡((1+tan2⁡θ)k0​ξ)>ε1/12\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\right)>\varepsilon^{1/12} and (1+tan2⁡θ)k0​ξ∈𝔅r\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r} as claimed. ∎

V.1 Upper bound of ‖V‖2\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2}, Eq. 63.

Let us write R1​k,k=1,…​2​n,R_{1k},k=1,\ldots 2n, and R2​l,l=1,…​2​n,R_{2l},l=1,\ldots 2n, for the entries of the vector R1=(Q1,P1,…,Qn,Pn)R_{1}=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{n},P_{n}) and R2=(Qn+1,Pn+1,…,Q2​n,P2​n)R_{2}=(Q_{n+1},P_{n+1},\ldots,Q_{2n},P_{2n}) respectively. First, from the orthogonality of the symplectic matrix σ\sigma

‖V‖2\displaystyle\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2} =‖σ⁡(Tr⁡g​R1​R2T)​σT‖2|tan⁡θ|\displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert\sigma(\Tr gR_{1}R_{2}^{T})\sigma^{T}\right\rVert_{2}}{|\tan\theta|}
=‖Tr⁡g​R1​R2T‖2|tan⁡θ|=(∑k​l|Tr⁡g​R1​k​R2​l|2)1/2|tan⁡θ|.\displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert\Tr gR_{1}R_{2}^{T}\right\rVert_{2}}{|\tan\theta|}=\frac{\left(\sum_{kl}|\Tr gR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}}{|\tan\theta|}.

Our plan is to bound each entry |Tr⁡g​R1​k​R2​l|2|\Tr gR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2}. Since the operator gg is the difference of two Schwartz operators it is also Schwartz. Thus we have from Theorem 13 (i​i​i)−(i​v)(iii)-(iv) that |g|1/2|g|^{1/2} is a Schwartz operator. If g=∑λi​|i⟩​⟨i|g=\sum\lambda_{i}|i\rangle\langle i| is the spectral decomposition of gg, we consider the following factorization

g=|g|Q,withQ:=∑isgn⁡(λi)​|i⟩​⟨i|.g=|g|Q,\qquad\text{with}\qquad Q:=\sum_{i}\sgn(\lambda_{i})|i\rangle\langle i|.

Clearly, Q=Q−1Q=Q^{-1} commutes with |g||g| and |g|1/2|g|^{1/2}. Moreover, from Theorem 13 (i)(i) we will be able to use the trace cyclicity for our following computation. Using twice the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and ‖g‖1≤3​ε\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\varepsilon, we find

|Tr⁡g​R1​k​R2​l|2=|Tr⁡|g|1/2​|g|1/2​Q​R1​k​R2​l|2\displaystyle|\Tr gR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2}=|\Tr|g|^{1/2}|g|^{1/2}QR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2} ≤(Tr⁡|g|)​(Tr⁡|g|​R1​k2​R2​l2),\displaystyle\leq\left(\Tr|g|\right)\left(\Tr|g|R^{2}_{1k}R^{2}_{2l}\right),
≤3​ε​Tr⁡|g|​R1​k4​Tr​|g|​R2​l4,\displaystyle\leq 3\varepsilon\sqrt{\Tr|g|R^{4}_{1k}\Tr|g|R^{4}_{2l}},
≤(3​ε)​max​{Tr⁡|g|​R1​k4,Tr⁡|g|​R2​l4}.\displaystyle\leq(3\varepsilon)\max\{\Tr|g|R^{4}_{1k},\Tr|g|R^{4}_{2l}\}.

Using again the decomposition of gg we obtain for j=1,2j=1,2 that

|Tr|​g​|Rj​k4|=|Tr⁡Q​g​R4|≤‖Q‖​‖g​Rj​k4‖1\displaystyle|\Tr|g|R^{4}_{jk}|=|\Tr QgR^{4}|\leq\left\lVert Q\right\rVert\left\lVert gR^{4}_{jk}\right\rVert_{1} =‖(ρa​b−ρa⊗ρb)​Rj​k4‖1\displaystyle=\left\lVert(\rho_{ab}-\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b})R^{4}_{jk}\right\rVert_{1}
≤2​‖ρa​b​Rj​k4‖1,\displaystyle\leq 2\left\lVert\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{jk}\right\rVert_{1},

since Rj​k4R^{4}_{jk} is a local operator on one part of the output. Consequently, |Tr⁡g​R1​k​R2​l|2≤6​ε​max​{Tr⁡ρa​b​R1​k4,Tr⁡ρa​b​R2​l4}≤6​ε​κ|\Tr gR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2}\leq 6\varepsilon\max\{\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{1k},\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{2l}\}\leq 6\varepsilon\kappa where κ:=max⁡{‖ρa​b​Rξ2​Rη2‖1|‖ξ‖2=‖η‖2=1}\kappa:=\max\left\{\left\lVert\rho_{ab}R^{2}_{\xi}R^{2}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{1}\;\big|\;\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{2}=1\right\} is the largest generalized fourth moment of ρa​b\rho_{ab}. Note that since ρa​b\rho_{ab} is a Schwartz operator κ<∞\kappa<\infty. Thus

‖V‖2≤24​n2​κ​ε|tan⁡θ|.\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{24n^{2}\kappa\varepsilon}}{|\tan\theta|}.

V.2 Upper bound of |F⁡(ξ)||F(\xi)|, Eq. 64.

The line integral of a matrix A∈ℂ2​n×2​nA\in\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n} is defined in terms of the line integrals of the rows of AA. Namely, if Ak,k=1,…,2​nA_{k},k=1,\ldots,2n are the rows of AA, then

∫A⋅𝑑η:=(∫A1⋅𝑑η∫A2​n⋅𝑑η).\int A\cdot d\eta:=\begin{pmatrix}\int A_{1}\cdot d\eta\\ \vdots\\ \int A_{2n}\cdot d\eta\end{pmatrix}.

Thus the line integral of a matrix-valued function is a vector, and the line integral of a vector field is a scalar. Let us denote by M:ℝ2​n→ℂ2​n×2​nM:\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n} a matrix-valued function. The upper bound for Eq. 64 is equivalent to bound

F⁡(ξ):=∫𝒞⁡(ξ)(∫𝒞⁡(η)M⁡(z)⋅𝑑z)⋅𝑑η,F(\xi):=\int_{\mathcal{C}(\xi)}\left(\int_{\mathcal{C}(\eta)}M(z)\cdot dz\right)\cdot d\eta,

with ξ,η∈𝔅r/2\xi,\eta\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2} and

M⁡(z)=cos2⁡θ⁡(Q22​(z)+Q12​(z)tan⁡θ).M(z)=\cos^{2}\theta\left(Q_{22}(z)+\frac{Q_{12}(z)}{\tan\theta}\right).

Let us parametrize the curve 𝒞⁡(ξ)\mathcal{C}(\xi) via ϑ:[0,1]→𝒞\vartheta:[0,1]\to\mathcal{C}, t↦t​ξt\mapsto t\xi and write Mk​l​(z)M_{kl}(z) for the entries of the matrix M⁡(z)∈ℂ2​n×2​nM(z)\in\comp^{2n\times 2n}. Define the matrix-valued function ℝ2​n∋z↦Y⁡(z)∈ℂ2​n×2​n\reals^{2n}\ni z\mapsto Y(z)\in\comp^{2n\times 2n} to have the entries Yk​l​(z):=∫01Mk​l​(s​z)​𝑑sY_{kl}(z):=\int_{0}^{1}M_{kl}(sz)ds. From the explicit parametrization of the line integrals and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we obtain that

|F⁡(ξ)|\displaystyle|F(\xi)| ≤maxt∈[0,1]⁡|t​ξ⋅Y⁡(t​ξ)​ξ|,\displaystyle\leq\max_{t\in[0,1]}\left|t\xi\cdot Y(t\xi)\xi\right|,
≤‖ξ‖22​maxt∈[0,1]​(∑k,l=12​n|Y​(t​ξ)k​l|2)1/2.\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}_{2}\;\max_{t\in[0,1]}\left(\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}|Y(t\xi)_{kl}|^{2}\right)^{1/2}. (85)

In order to bound |Y​(t​ξ)k​l||Y(t\xi)_{kl}| we differentiate Eq. (51) with the help of Lemma 14 to find

Q22​(z)=G2​(z)​G2T​(z)χ12​(cos⁡θ​z)​χ22​(−sin⁡θ​z)−G22​(z)χ1​(cos⁡θ​z)​χ2​(−sin⁡θ​z)∈ℂ2​n×2​n,Q_{22}(z)=\frac{G_{2}(z)G^{T}_{2}(z)}{\chi^{2}_{1}(\cos\theta z)\chi^{2}_{2}(-\sin\theta z)}-\frac{G_{22}(z)}{\chi_{1}(\cos\theta z)\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta z)}\in\comp^{2n\times 2n},
